title: Med Spa Referral Program: Rewards, Rules and Tracking (2026)
summary: Build a med spa referral program that works: pick the reward, decide when it is earned, track who referred whom and stay inside the rules for medical services.
body_markdown:
## What a Med Spa Referral Program Is and Why It Pays Back


A med spa referral program is a written offer that rewards an existing patient when someone they recommend becomes a paying patient. It pays back because the people you reach are already warm: they were told about you by someone they trust, and you did not pay an ad platform for the click.


That matters for the budget. Our own[med spa marketing guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-marketing-guide) treats existing patients as the lowest-cost acquisition channel, and the[KPIs worth tracking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-kpi-tracking) include how many new patients came from word of mouth. A program gives that channel a number.


It also protects the work you have already done. Patients refer when the visit went well and they are reminded at the right time. A clinic that already runs strong[retention and rebooking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-retention-and-rebooking) has more happy patients to ask, so the program multiplies something that exists.


## Referral Program Ideas Compared


Most med spa referral programs use one of four reward structures: a credit for the referrer, a credit for both sides, a tiered reward that grows with each referral, or points that accumulate. Pick the simplest one your front desk can explain in a sentence.


Top-ranking guides agree on the basic menu and on one warning: programs with long lists of exclusions, minimum spends or confusing steps tend to be ignored by the patients you want to reach. The table shows the trade-off in each.


Structure Example Best for Watch out for


Referrer credit only $50 credit after the friend's first paid visit Clinics starting out, small budgets Referrers may feel awkward asking for a favor


Two-sided credit $25 for the referrer and $25 for the friend Clinics that want more invitations sent The friend's credit is also a discount, so check it against your[discount policy](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-discount-policy)


Tiered reward Higher credit for the third and fifth referral Patients who already love you Harder to track by hand, and it needs a cap


Points Points toward any service, redeemed later Clinics already running loyalty Points are a liability until spent, so set the conversion once


Professional partners Shared first-visit offer with a salon or dental office Clinics with complementary neighbors Cash payments between businesses raise legal questions


A clinic that gave a $100 credit per referral told us it was unsure where staff should record "referred by" and whether the credit could happen automatically. Those are the right two questions, and the rest of this guide answers them.


## Choose a Reward That Fits the First-Visit Ticket


Set the reward as a fixed account credit that equals a modest share of what a new patient spends on a first visit. If a typical first visit is $300, a $25 to $50 credit keeps the cost of acquiring a patient well below what you would pay for a paid click.


Credit beats cash for three reasons. It brings the referrer back, it carries no payout cost until it is redeemed, and it avoids handing out money in exchange for a recommendation for a medical service. Gift cards sit in between, but a cash-like reward invites more questions from a regulator than credit toward your own treatments does.


Give the credit an expiry date, usually 90 days, and say so in the offer. Stored credit is a liability on your books until it is used, which is the same reasoning behind our advice on[package credits and refunds](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-package-refund-policy) . An open-ended credit that never expires is easy to promise and hard to carry.


Keep the amount fixed instead of a percentage. A percentage creates a different number on every referral, and the front desk has to calculate it at the counter.


## Decide When the Reward Is Earned


A referral should earn its reward when the referred patient completes a first paid visit. Paying at booking turns every cancellation and no-show into a loss, and the booking is the step with the highest drop-off.


Spell out the trigger in three lines that staff can read aloud:


- The referred person is a new patient, with no earlier visit or purchase.
- Their first appointment is completed and paid.
- The referrer is not the patient, a member of their household, or an employee.


Some clinics use a booking trigger because it feels faster and rewards the referrer sooner. If you do, pay only after the visit and send a message at booking that says the credit is on its way. The referrer still gets feedback, and you do not pay for an appointment that never happened.


The hard cases are small. A patient who refers two friends in the same week, a friend who books for the next month, a referral that arrives through a different family member's account: decide each once and write down the answer, so staff are not deciding at the counter.


## Track Who Referred Whom


The only reliable way to track referrals is to record the referrer on the new patient's profile at the moment they sign up, using a unique link, a code or a required question on the intake form. A note on a credit tells you who was paid, not who brought in whom.


Each method has a place:


- **Unique links.** Each patient gets a personal link to your booking page. Attribution is automatic and the patient does not have to remember anything.
- **Codes.** A short code the friend enters or says at the desk. Easy to share verbally and on a card, but prone to typos.
- **A required intake question.** "Were you referred by someone? Who?" is the fallback, and it catches walk-ins and people who ignored the link.


Use the intake question even if you use links. Patients mention a friend after they have already booked, and the question is the only place that mention is captured. Pull the answers into the same report as your other lead sources, so referrals sit next to paid ads in your[lead source tracking](https://decodahealth.com/blog/google-meta-ads-lead-tracking-practice) .


Manual credit still works for a handful of referrals a month, particularly when a staff member verifies each one. The failure point is the name: one person writes a first name, another writes a nickname, and you cannot match them months later. If you stay manual, use a fixed note format such as "Referral: \[referrer name\], \[new patient name\], \[date\]" and keep it identical.


## Stay Inside the Rules for Medical Services


For cash-pay aesthetic services a patient referral reward is generally allowed, but the rules differ by state and by service, and anything touching a federal health care program changes the answer. Have a healthcare attorney review the offer before launch.


Three rule sets come up most often:


- **Federal Anti-Kickback Statute.** It makes it a crime to offer or pay anything of value to induce referrals of items or services paid by a Federal health care program. Cash-pay aesthetics usually sit outside it, but a clinic that bills Medicare or Medicaid for any service does not. The text is in[42 U.S.C. 1320a-7b](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1320a-7b) .
- **State rules on medical services.** Some states restrict discounts or rewards tied to medical treatments such as injectables or prescription therapies, and some limit fee-sharing with outside parties. Guides from other vendors flag Texas, New York, Florida and California as states to check.
- **Advertising and endorsements.** When someone is rewarded for recommending you publicly, the connection should be disclosed. The FTC's[endorsement guidance](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing/endorsements-influencers-reviews) says that applies when an endorser has been paid or given something of value. Do not tie a reward to a public review or a positive rating.


Messaging is its own item. If your program asks patients to text friends or you text the referrer about their reward, the consent rules in our guide to[med spa text message consent](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-text-message-consent) and in[47 CFR 64.1200](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/47/64.1200) apply. Never post or share a referred patient's name or visit details; the program records who referred whom, not what treatment anyone had.


## Prevent Self-Referrals and Duplicate Rewards


Most referral abuse is simple: a patient refers themselves with a second email, or the same referral is rewarded twice. Both are prevented by a written definition of a qualified referral and a monthly review of rewards paid.


Three habits cover almost all of it. Match new patients against existing profiles by name, phone and date of birth before you pay. Cap the number of paid referral rewards per person per year if you want a ceiling. And check that a reward granted automatically is not also granted by hand, since two staff members rewarding the same referral is the most common duplicate we hear about.


A monthly report with four columns is enough: referrer, new patient, first paid visit date and credit issued. If the list is longer than you can read in five minutes, the program is working and it is time to automate.


## Write the Offer Patients Will Understand


The offer should fit in two sentences on a card, a text or a receipt, with the reward, the trigger and the expiry stated plainly. "Refer a friend. When they complete their first visit, you get a $50 credit that lasts 90 days."


Put the details in a short terms line: new patients only, one reward per new patient, credit toward services, no cash value. That line protects you when a patient asks for exceptions and keeps staff from improvising.


Then decide when you ask. The best moments are right after a good result, at checkout and in the follow-up message a few days later. Our guide to[aftercare instructions](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-aftercare-instructions) covers the follow-up message you can reuse, and asking for the referral in the same thread feels natural. Ask for a review in a separate message; our post on[med spa review requests](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-review-requests) explains why mixing the two lowers the response to both.


## How Decoda Health Handles Referrals


Decoda Health includes a Referral Programs setting under Settings, then Growth, where you choose an account-credit promotion as the reward for the referring patient and set the rule that makes a referred patient qualify. Attribution works through referral links, and a reward for the referred patient is optional.


The qualification rule is the part that matters. It lets a clinic pay the referrer after the friend books, completes a visit or makes a purchase, depending on how the rule is set, so the reward follows the trigger you wrote in your policy instead of someone remembering to add it. Clinics that want to keep verifying referrals themselves can still add a credit by hand in billing with a clear note, which is a reasonable choice at low volume.


Credits issued this way sit alongside the rest of the patient's balance, so they can be spent at checkout the same way as other account credit. If you run recurring plans too, see how[VIP memberships and patient wallets](https://decodahealth.com/blog/setting-up-vip-memberships-beauty-banks-and-patient-wallets) handle balances, and the[Decoda Growth tools](https://decodahealth.com/products/growth) for the campaigns that remind patients to refer.


Which patients can open the Referral Programs page depends on the clinic's access settings, so ask your onboarding contact to confirm it before you plan a launch around it.


## Measure Whether the Program Pays Back


A referral program pays back when the lifetime spend of a referred patient comfortably exceeds the reward and the time staff spend running it. Track four numbers each month: referrals received, referrals that qualified, rewards issued and revenue from referred patients.


Divide rewards issued by the number of qualified referrals to get the cost per new patient, then compare it with what you pay for a lead from ads. If a $50 credit brings in a patient you would otherwise pay $150 to reach, the program is cheap. If your qualified rate is low, the invitation is reaching people who never intended to book, and the fix is in how you ask.


Also watch the referrers. A small group of patients usually accounts for most referrals. Thank them in a way that is more personal than a credit, such as early access to a new treatment or a note from the injector. The spreadsheet will show you who they are.


Review the program every quarter: keep the reward if the cost per patient is below paid channels, raise it for the referrers who produce the most, and remove any rule staff have to keep explaining.


## Final Thoughts on Running a Med Spa Referral Program


A med spa referral program is a small system: one reward, one trigger, one place where the referrer is recorded, and a monthly look at what was paid. Write those four things down before you tell a single patient about it.


Start with referrer credit only, pay after the first completed visit, and review the offer with your attorney. Add a friend credit or tiers once the basics hold for a quarter. ## Frequently Asked Questions


What is a good reward for a med spa referral program?


A fixed account credit of $25 to $100 is the most common choice, paid to the patient who referred and, optionally, to the new patient. Credit works better than cash because it brings the referrer back for another visit and avoids paying out money for a medical service. Keep the amount at a small share of the average first-visit ticket so the program stays profitable.


When should a med spa pay out a referral reward?


Pay after the referred patient has completed their first paid visit, not when they book. Bookings get cancelled and no-showed, and a reward paid at booking turns every cancellation into a loss. If you want faster feedback for the referrer, send a thank-you message at booking and say the credit arrives after the visit.


How do you track patient referrals in a med spa?


Use a unique referral link or code for each patient when you can, and a required "referred by" field on intake forms when you cannot. A free-text note on a credit works for a handful of referrals a month but breaks down once several staff members enter names differently. Whatever you choose, record the referrer on the new patient's profile so you can report on it.


Is it legal to pay patients for referrals at a med spa?


For cash-pay aesthetic services it is generally allowed, but the rules differ by state and by service. The federal Anti-Kickback Statute covers referrals for items paid by federal health care programs, and some states restrict rewards tied to medical treatments. Ask your healthcare attorney to review the offer before launch, and keep rewards as credit toward your own services.


Should the new patient get a reward too?


A reward for the new patient is optional, but it usually helps the referrer feel like they are giving a gift instead of selling. A smaller welcome credit for the friend, redeemable on a first treatment, makes the invitation easier to send. If margins are tight, reward only the referrer and put the budget into a better thank-you.


How do you stop people from gaming a referral program?


Define a qualified referral in writing: a new patient who has never been treated, whose first paid visit is completed, and who is not the referrer's household member or the referrer. Cap the rewards per person per year if you need to, and review the list of paid rewards monthly. Most abuse is self-referral and duplicate profiles, and both show up when someone looks.
